profiles.meeting_scenario: A law firm is holding a design review of a draft client-facing due-diligence memo and disclosure schedule for a private equity client considering an acquisition of a DeFi lending platform. The draft memo explains how the client may rely on Solicitous/SMTChecker results when describing the target's Solidity contracts as "formally verified" in diligence materials and, later, in transaction disclosures. The agenda is to review whether the memo's structure, caveats, and exceptions schedule are sufficient for partner approval. The expected outcome is a decision on whether the draft is ready for client circulation with minor edits, or whether it needs additional revisions before approval.

members.name: Elena Park
members.expertise: Acquisition diligence, disclosure drafting, and legal opinions for digital asset and software-heavy deals
members.background: Elena leads the firm's blockchain M&A practice and regularly converts technical diligence into transaction-ready disclosure language for boards, lenders, and buyers.
members.private_state: She wants a usable, commercially readable memo approved quickly so the client can keep the acquisition timeline on track, and she is wary of technical caveats expanding into a document that undermines deal confidence.
hidden_assumptions: "Formally verified" is a disclosure phrase of art that can fairly describe a contract if the core economic-risk properties have been proven, even if the claim is not mathematically exhaustive.
When the diligence packet refers to "the deployed contract," it ordinarily means the business-logic implementation supplied in the data room, unless someone flags a specific mismatch.
Technical modeling assumptions are mainly support for the legal team and do not all need to appear in the client-facing exceptions schedule.
A memo is "ready to circulate" once its legal framing is stable and any remaining factual inserts can be filled from the existing diligence materials.

members.name: Daniel Ruiz
members.role: Counsel, Blockchain Risk and Digital Assets
members.expertise: Smart-contract diligence, formal verification claims, and technical-to-legal risk translation
members.background: Daniel is a former software engineer turned lawyer who reviews audit reports, compiler artifacts, and on-chain deployment details for digital asset transactions and regulatory responses.
members.private_state: He wants to prevent the firm from overstating what the verification results actually establish, and he is especially concerned about legal language drifting away from the exact artifact, property set, and model assumptions used by the verifier.
hidden_assumptions: "Formally verified" should be used only for specifically enumerated safety properties proven over the exact deployed artifact or its bytecode-equivalent source build.
"The deployed contract" means the on-chain address set actually handling value, including any proxy structure and control contracts materially affecting execution.
Model assumptions such as trusted token behavior, compiler-version matching, and proxy/admin invariants are material limitations that belong in the client-facing exceptions schedule.
A memo is not "ready to circulate" until the verification results have been reconciled against the exact compiler version, settings, and deployed configuration referenced in the draft.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both members comfortably use the phrase "formally verified" when discussing the draft memo.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the memo may describe the target as formally verified if key safety properties relevant to deal risk have been established for the core Solidity contract, with ordinary legal caveats.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the phrase should only refer to a narrow, technical claim: certain listed properties were proven for a precisely identified artifact under stated assumptions.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase is common in both legal and technical diligence conversations, so each hears a familiar, professionally acceptable meaning and assumes the other is invoking the same standard without needing to unpack it.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both members refer to "the deployed contract" and "the production deployment" as if they are discussing the same object.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the implementation contract file in the diligence packet, specifically the VaultV3 Solidity source the target identifies as the production contract.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the live mainnet deployment set: the proxy address receiving user funds, the linked implementation, and the proxy admin/control path that can alter behavior.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In transaction practice, people often speak of a software system in singular form for convenience, and neither side expects that shorthand to conceal different underlying referents.

misalignment_points.topic: What belongs in the exceptions schedule
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that the memo should include an "exceptions schedule" covering the verification assumptions.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the schedule should include only concise, client-salient carveouts such as properties not proven or obvious tooling limitations that materially affect the legal conclusion.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the schedule should also include modeling assumptions and environmental conditions such as trusted ERC-20 behavior, compiler pinning, proxy invariants, and other technical preconditions for the proof.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: An exceptions schedule sounds like a settled document category in legal drafting, so both treat its boundaries as obvious and continue refining content without realizing they are using different inclusion rules.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means for the draft to be "ready to circulate"
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether the memo will be "ready to circulate" after the current round of edits.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the document is circulation-ready if the legal analysis, caveat structure, and disclosure framing are complete enough to send to the client while minor factual details are finalized from existing materials.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the document is circulation-ready only after a technical confirmation step: rerunning or reconciling Solicitous results against the exact solc version and deployment configuration tied to mainnet.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In internal legal review, "ready to circulate" often functions as a routine milestone rather than a formally defined gate, so each person silently supplies their own completion threshold.

The memo's legal framing is basically there, and I do not want another round of technical expansion to spook the client or slow the deal. If the structure is stable and the remaining inserts can be drawn from the diligence packet, it's ready to circulate this week.
